clue.text: Be critical about an expert able to solve everything

indicators.note: the word for being critical goes round the other pieces, split to enclose them

parts.note: to pan something is to criticise it harshly
taken as written
an ace is an expert or star performer

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to criticise a specialist who claims to fix every problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for being critical is split around the other two pieces, its first letter on one side and the rest on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a cure-all, so the adjective describes something able to remedy or resolve every difficulty.

clue.text: Carries on without leader a long time, however short (as 13)

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for carrying on is dropped

parts.note: to wage a war is to carry it on

explanation.surface: Someone persists for a stretch that turns out brief after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes Chambers (13 is IN CHAMBERS), whose entry for ages says a long time, however short; 'Carries on' tempts toward RAGES, but it is WAGES as in waging war.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers's dictionary entry for the plural noun, playfully admitting that a period called endless is often brief.

clue.text: Menial servant of duke, character in Dickens

parts.note: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel

explanation.surface: A ducal household's lowly servant turns out to be a figure from Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: A drudge is a person made to do dull, servile work, a lowly menial.

clue.text: Brief one's put in front of court previously

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word court is taken
the letters for one's are placed inside the word for previously

parts.note: once means at an earlier time
one is I, and 's stands for is, giving I plus S

explanation.surface: A short legal note says someone was placed before the court earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's' is read as I plus 'S for 'is'; the answer is also the name of an Oxford dictionary, paired with 21-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something short and to the point, using few words; it is also the name of an Oxford dictionary.

clue.text: Get to know about awfully obese wit

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters are in a terrible mess and need reshuffling

explanation.surface: Someone learns of a dreadfully fat comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' rearranges OBESEWIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To be wise to something is an idiom meaning to have become aware of or learned about it.

clue.text: Lie blandly when wrong — it'll get one nowhere

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Telling a smooth lie when you are mistaken is a futile course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges LIEBLANDLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead-end street leads nowhere, and figuratively the phrase names any course of action with no prospect of success.

clue.text: Heartlessly bitter clue for author of diabolical 11

indicators.note: the central letters of each of the two words bitter and clue are removed

explanation.surface: A harsh, unkind hint about a writer of a devilish reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessly' strips the middle TT from bitter, giving BIER, and the middle LU from clue, giving CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrose Bierce, the American satirist, wrote The Devil's Dictionary, a wickedly cynical lexicon.

clue.text: Mother and son in novel by Lawrence

parts.note: Kanga is the mother ... in A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories
Roo is Kanga's young son in the same books

explanation.surface: A mother and her son feature in a book by D. H. Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Lawrence's Sons and Lovers, with its intense mother and son; instead the pair are Milne's Kanga and Roo.
explanation.definitionFit: Kangaroo is a 1923 novel by D. H. Lawrence set in Australia.

clue.text: Destroyed a relic that's long in shape but short in duration, as 13

definitions.text: long in shape but short in duration, as 13

indicators.note: a destroyed object is wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wrecked an antique that was oblong but did not last long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyed' rearranges ARELIC; the definition is Chambers's famous entry for the pastry (13 is IN CHAMBERS).
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers defines the cream-filled choux pastry as long in shape but short in duration, since it is eaten quickly.

clue.text: Fare for Scots and English stable, according to self-proclaimed 16 3

definitions.text: Fare for Scots and English stable, according to self-proclaimed 16 3

parts.words: Fare for Scots and English stable, according to self-proclaimed 16 3
parts.note: Johnson, who called a lexicographer a harmless drudge, defined this grain as one given to horses in England but which in Scotland supports the people

explanation.surface: A dictionary-maker's sly remark on what Scots eat and English horses get.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 3 is HARMLESS DRUDGE, Samuel Johnson's own description of a lexicographer; his dictionary entry for this cereal was a famous jibe at the Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: The cereal grain is porridge food in Scotland and horse feed in English stables, as Johnson's definition mocked.

clue.text: Altered road in city such as 4 21, 17, or 22 down

indicators.note: altered means changed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A street in town was changed, like several well-known names listed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Altered' rearranges ROADINCITY; the examples are CONCISE OXFORD, COLLINS and BREWER, all reference books.
explanation.definitionFit: Concise Oxford, Collins and Brewer's are all names of well-known reference books listing words and meanings.

clue.text: Do some work for 11, putting some fish in river

indicators.note: the part of a fish is placed inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another flows through Wales and England
a fin is part of a fish

explanation.surface: Someone helps a reference work by dropping a bit of fish into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some fish' gives only a part of a fish, its fin, not a species; the river is the Dee.
explanation.definitionFit: Explaining the meaning of words is the core labour of compiling a lexicon.

clue.text: Move cautiously with warning signals, where some cases are heard

parts.note: to inch is to move slowly and carefully
amber traffic lights are warnings

explanation.surface: A driver creeps forward as the lights turn amber.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase also names the Chambers dictionary that the puzzle keeps quoting.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal matters heard privately by a judge rather than in open court are said to be dealt with in the judge's private rooms.

clue.text: For what's defined as "lots of percolated liquids" refer to other places

parts.note: see is the instruction used to refer readers onward
pages are the other places in a book a reader is sent to

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry cross-refers the reader elsewhere instead of defining.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a book's cross-reference, 'see pages' sends you to other places; the definition is in the style of a dictionary entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A leakage that slowly oozes through is a seepage, and the plural covers many such trickling liquids.

clue.text: Italian dish it's no good returning, with badly limited choice

indicators.note: the abbreviation for no good is read backwards
badly signals the trimmed letters are rearranged
limited means the word is cut short, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A restaurant critic complains that a poorly stocked menu offers nothing good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns NG into GN; 'limited' cuts choice to CHOIC, which 'badly' rearranges into OCCHI.
explanation.definitionFit: The small potato dumplings are a classic Italian dish.

clue.text: Husband with weapon not so benign

parts.note: an arm is a weapon
less means not so much

explanation.surface: A man with a gun is said to be not so gentle after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson called a lexicographer a harmless drudge, linking this to 3.
explanation.definitionFit: Something benign is gentle and causes no injury or damage.

clue.text: Novelist making change, inserting lines

indicators.note: the abbreviation for lines is placed inside the word for making change

parts.note: to coin money is to make it, as coins are change

explanation.surface: A writer revises a manuscript by putting in extra lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is also that of a dictionary publisher, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins wrote The Woman in White and The Moonstone.

clue.text: Lots of points about nothing in "the objections that are urged against this excellent 11" (see 7's 11)

definitions.text: the objections that are urged against this excellent 11

indicators.note: the compass letters go around the zero

parts.note: N, N, S, E, N, S and E are compass points
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Numerous compass bearings surround a quotation about a fine dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is Bierce's entry in The Devil's Dictionary, as '(see 7's 11)' tells you.
explanation.definitionFit: Bierce's satirical dictionary defines the word for absurd rubbish as the objections made against his own fine book.

clue.text: Policy covering aliens and some of their homes

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece covering another sits on top of it

parts.note: a plan is a policy or course of action
ETs are extraterrestrials, aliens from space

explanation.surface: A government strategy that deals with outsiders and where they live.
explanation.definitionFit: Worlds orbiting stars are where aliens would live, so they are their homes.

clue.text: Work of art covering acceptable area, like a Van Gogh self-portrait?

indicators.note: the word for the artwork goes around the other two pieces

parts.note: a mural is a painting on a wall
on means acceptable, as in that's just not on

explanation.surface: A painting showing a decent space, perhaps of a famous Dutch painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Van Gogh cut off part of his ear, so his self-portrait shows him with one ear only.
explanation.definitionFit: The word strictly means with one ear, or one channel of sound; Van Gogh famously lost part of an ear.

clue.text: Old president holding vote in Mississippi city

indicators.note: the old president's letters enclose the mark for a vote

parts.note: Gerald Ford was a US president
X is the mark made on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A former president keeps a ballot in a Southern US city.
explanation.walkthrough: The name also belongs to the famous dictionary, here paired with 4 as CONCISE OXFORD.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford is a city in Mississippi, home of the state university.

clue.text: Better than what's done by being silly

indicators.note: being silly suggests letters acting foolishly, out of their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone surpasses what is achieved by fooling around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being silly' rearranges DONEBY.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition means exceeding or surpassing, as in beyond expectation.

clue.text: Supplier of porters we're changing in old transport system

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the abbreviation for the railway

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the former UK national railway

indicators.note: changing signals the letters of we're are rearranged

explanation.surface: Railway porters change shifts on the old national railway system.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter is a dark beer, not a railway worker, despite the old railway in the clue; Brewer's is also a phrase dictionary, hence its place in 11.
explanation.definitionFit: Porter is a dark beer, so a beer-maker supplies porters; Brewer's is also a dictionary of phrase and fable.

clue.text: Unsteady old king pierced by British weapon

indicators.note: the letter for British is driven into the king's name

parts.note: Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia
a lance is a long spear

explanation.surface: An ancient king, stabbed with a British spear, totters.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa, the Mercian king who built Offa's Dyke, is a crossword staple for 'old king'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught off balance means being unsteady and liable to fall.

clue.text: Reproduced book with colour added

parts.note: red is a colour

explanation.surface: A book is reprinted with coloured ink added.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that reproduced have bred, the past tense of breed.

clue.text: Put up with a person who talks when you wish him to listen, according to 7

definitions.meaning: the past tense of bear, to tolerate

definitions.text: a person who talks when you wish him to listen, according to 7
definitions.meaning: Bierce's Devil's Dictionary definition of a tedious person

explanation.surface: A bore defined by a cynic as the man who won't stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is BIERCE; the second definition quotes his Devil's Dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of bear means tolerated; as a noun it is a tiresome, tedious talker.

clue.text: Huge numbers in India holding rupees in central parts

indicators.note: the word for central parts encloses the abbreviation for the currency

parts.note: cores are the centres of things

explanation.surface: Large sums in Indian money sit at the heart of things.
explanation.definitionFit: In India a crore is ten million, so the plural means huge numbers.

clue.text: Supposedly lucky types, fair people who never speak well of one another (Johnson)

definitions.text: fair people who never speak well of one another (Johnson)
definitions.meaning: Samuel Johnson said ... are a fair people, for they never speak well of one another

explanation.surface: A nation said to be fortunate and quick to criticise each other.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's quip uses fair to mean just: they are honest about each other's faults.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Ireland are proverbially lucky, and Johnson famously called them a fair people.
